name: Report and review patient safety incidents
summary: Staff who see a patient safety incident or near miss give immediate care and then enter a report in the hospital's safety reporting system. A quality specialist screens new reports each business day and the unit manager follows up and closes most of them, but serious harm is escalated at once for a preliminary review, disclosure to the patient, a concise or comprehensive analysis, an approved action plan and, for critical incidents, reports to the Medical Advisory Committee, the board quality committee and, for medication events, a provincial reporting system. Delays come from managers' follow-up queues, booking review teams and committee calendars, and under-reporting and weak actions limit what the hospital learns.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation with about 640 beds, a quality and risk team of about 20 and a commercial web-based incident reporting system used by all staff.
baseline.notes: Ontario rules: Public Hospitals Act Regulation 965 on critical incident disclosure and review, the 2011 ministry directive on NSIR reporting of medication critical incidents, the Quality of Care Information Protection Act and Accreditation Canada required practices.

trigger: A staff member, physician or volunteer sees a patient safety incident or near miss and enters a report.
end_state: The report is followed up and closed by the manager, or, for serious harm, the analysis is done, the patient has been told, actions are tracked to completion, required committee and external reports are filed and the file is closed.

volume.seasonality: Fairly even; slightly higher in winter when census and staffing pressure are highest.

evidence.note: A mandatory statewide system recorded 27.9 hospital event reports per 1,000 patient days in 2022; at 17,500-19,500 patient days a month that is about 490-540 reports, plus reports from 13,000 emergency visits and outpatient areas a month. Agrees with the organisation file range; Ontario reporting is voluntary and may be lower.
Front-line staff (mostly nurses) give immediate care, tell the charge nurse and enter the report. Represented by the inpatient RN role; FTE is the author's estimate of that time across all reporters.
Patient care managers for medicine, mental health, maternity and other non-surgical units follow up reports from their units. Author's estimate.
Emergency department managers follow up reports from the three emergency departments. Author's estimate.

roles.title: Patient care manager, perioperative or surgical unit

evidence.note: Perioperative and surgical unit managers follow up reports from their units. Author's estimate.
Quality and patient safety specialists screen reports, facilitate analyses, prepare committee reports and file external reports. About 5 of the 8 specialists' time; author's estimate.

roles.title: Director, quality, risk and patient experience
roles.department: Quality, patient safety and professional practice

evidence.note: Director of quality decides review type, chairs quality of care reviews and approves action plans. Author's estimate of time.
Administrator on call is notified of significant harm after hours. Author's estimate of time.
The most responsible physician discloses harm to the patient; represented by the hospitalist role. Author's estimate of time.
Department chiefs join comprehensive reviews of critical incidents. Author's estimate.

systems.name: Safety incident and complaints reporting system
Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones
CIHI National System for Incident Reporting (web portal)

steps.name: Give immediate care and tell the charge nurse
steps.description: The nurse or other staff member who finds the incident (a fall, a wrong dose, a mislabelled specimen) checks the patient, gets the physician to assess if needed, tells the charge nurse and documents the facts of the event in the patient's chart without mentioning the incident report.

evidence.note: Immediate response duties from the CIAF and Ontario hospital policies. Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Enter the incident report
steps.description: Usually later in the shift, the staff member logs into the safety reporting system, picks the incident type, location and patient, writes what happened, rates the apparent harm and names any equipment or medication involved; the report goes to the unit manager.

error.defect_description: Incident type or harm level misclassified, or key facts missing.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada Required Organizational Practice: patient safety incident management

next.condition: no harm, near miss or minor harm
moderate or severe harm or death: leaders phoned at once

evidence.note: Reporting duty from Ontario policies; 3.8% of reports in a large mandatory system were harmful events. Time to report is the author's estimate.

steps.name: System routes the report
steps.description: The incident system files the report under the unit and incident type, emails the responsible manager and the quality team, and adds it to the manager's open follow-up queue.

evidence.note: Standard behaviour of hospital incident reporting systems in this period; author's knowledge.

steps.name: Quality specialist screens new reports
steps.description: Each business morning a quality and patient safety specialist reads the new reports, corrects the type or routing, checks the harm rating, and pulls out any that look more serious than rated for escalation.

error.defect_description: A serious event is left rated as minor.

next.condition: medicine, mental health, maternity or support unit

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice; unit shares follow the trigger shares in interfaces.

steps.name: Unit manager follows up (medicine and other units)
steps.description: The patient care manager opens the report from the incident system queue, talks to the staff involved and, where needed, the patient, confirms the harm level and contributing factors, records actions taken (staff coaching, equipment fix, process reminder) and marks the follow-up complete.

error.defect_description: Harm level left wrong or follow-up actions not documented.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada Required Organizational Practice: patient safety incident management

evidence.note: Author's estimate; slow manager follow-up is noted in the organisation file.

steps.name: Unit manager follows up (emergency)
steps.description: The emergency department patient care manager opens the report from the incident system queue, talks to the staff involved and, where needed, the patient, confirms the harm level and contributing factors, records actions taken (staff coaching, equipment fix, process reminder) and marks the follow-up complete.

error.defect_description: Harm level left wrong or follow-up actions not documented.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada Required Organizational Practice: patient safety incident management

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Unit manager follows up (surgery)
steps.description: The perioperative or surgical patient care manager opens the report from the incident system queue, talks to the staff involved and, where needed, the patient, confirms the harm level and contributing factors, records actions taken (staff coaching, equipment fix, process reminder) and marks the follow-up complete.

error.defect_description: Harm level left wrong or follow-up actions not documented.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada Required Organizational Practice: patient safety incident management

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Quality specialist checks and closes the report
steps.description: In a weekly pass the specialist checks that the follow-up is documented and the harm level and contributing factors are coded consistently for trend reports, then closes the report or sends it back to the manager.

next.condition: pattern or harm found that needs review

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Chase the manager for overdue follow-up
steps.description: The specialist emails or raises at the program quality meeting the reports still open past the hospital's target, and the manager adds the missing follow-up before the report comes back for checking.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Escalate to leaders and secure items
steps.description: For serious harm the charge nurse phones the manager or, after hours, the administrator on call, who makes sure the patient is safe, the physician and family are informed, and the equipment, medication or supplies involved are kept aside and tagged out of service.

control.basis: CIAF immediate response: secure items and reduce the risk of imminent recurrence; hospital remove-from-service (tag-out) procedure for equipment

evidence.note: Notification chain (administrator on call after 16:30 and on weekends) from QCH policy; secure items from the CIAF.

steps.name: Preliminary review of a serious incident
steps.description: A quality and patient safety specialist reads the chart and the report, phones the staff involved, decides whether the event meets the critical incident definition, and identifies whether a device or medication report to an outside body may be needed.

error.defect_description: Event wrongly judged not to be a critical incident.

evidence.note: Preliminary investigation step from the CIAF; Ontario critical incident definition. Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Physician discloses the incident to the patient
steps.description: The most responsible physician, with a nurse or manager present, meets the patient or family, explains what happened and its consequences, apologizes, says what will be done next and records the disclosure in the chart.

control.basis: Public Hospitals Act, Regulation 965 (hospital management): disclosure of critical incidents to the patient, the medical advisory committee and the administrator

evidence.note: Two-stage disclosure and chart documentation from the QCH policy; legal duty for critical incidents from Regulation 965 as described by the Auditor General.

steps.name: Director decides the type of review
steps.description: The director of quality reviews the preliminary findings and decides on a concise review led by one facilitator or a comprehensive review by a team, whether to run it as a protected quality of care review, and whether the insurer must be notified.

evidence.note: Concise versus comprehensive choice from the CIAF; QCIPA quality of care reviews from QCH policy. Shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Notify the insurer
steps.description: The specialist writes a short factual notice of the incident and the possible claim to the hospital's liability insurer and keeps the reference number on the incident file.

control.basis: Liability insurance subscription terms: prompt notice of incidents that may lead to a claim

evidence.note: The Auditor General lists the insurer (HIROC) as having access to incident cases. Notice practice and share are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Concise analysis
steps.description: The specialist, acting as facilitator, gathers the facts from the chart and short interviews with staff, the patient and family, identifies the main contributing factors and drafts actions with the unit manager over a few days.

evidence.note: Concise analysis by one facilitator over hours to days (CIAF Figure 3.8). Effort is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Set up the comprehensive review
steps.description: The specialist picks the review team (physician lead, managers, staff from the unit, an outside expert if needed), books interviews and a meeting room, and has members sign the quality of care confidentiality agreement.

evidence.note: Prepare-for-analysis stage: identify the team, coordinate meetings, plan interviews.

steps.name: Interview staff and build the timeline
steps.description: The specialist interviews the staff, physicians and patient or family involved, collects policies, equipment logs and orders, and builds a timeline and contributing factor diagram for the team.

evidence.note: Interviews and timeline from the CIAF analysis process. Effort is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Chair the quality of care review meeting
steps.description: The director of quality chairs the protected review meeting, walks the team through the timeline, and leads the discussion of how and why the incident happened and which system changes would prevent it.

control.basis: Public Hospitals Act, Regulation 965 (hospital management): disclosure of critical incidents to the patient, the medical advisory committee and the administrator

evidence.note: Committee review of every critical incident and QCIPA quality of care committee from the Auditor General; comprehensive analysis up to 90 days from the CIAF.

steps.name: Physician leaders take part in the review
steps.description: Two department chiefs or physician leads from the services involved attend the same meeting, explain the clinical decisions and agree the medical findings and recommendations.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of team composition.

steps.name: Unit managers take part in the review
steps.description: Two managers or educators from the units involved attend the same meeting, describe staffing, equipment and workflow on the day and take on actions for their units.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of team composition.

steps.name: Draft recommendations and action plan
steps.description: The specialist writes the findings, contributing factors and recommended actions with an owner and due date for each, using the hierarchy of effectiveness to favour system fixes over reminders.

error.defect_description: Actions rely on education and reminders that do not change the system.

evidence.note: Develop and manage recommended actions (CIAF).

steps.name: Director approves the action plan
steps.description: The director of quality reviews the action plan with the program director, confirms owners and dates, and signs it off for tracking.

control.basis: Hospital incident management policy: leadership approval of recommendations

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Disclose findings and system changes to the patient
steps.description: The physician, with the manager or director, meets or phones the patient or family to share the facts learned and the system steps the hospital is taking, within what a protected quality of care review allows, and records the date in the chart.

control.basis: Public Hospitals Act, Regulation 965 (hospital management): disclosure of critical incidents to the patient, the medical advisory committee and the administrator

evidence.note: Post-analysis (second stage) disclosure from the QCH policy; disclosure of systemic steps for critical incidents under Regulation 965.

steps.name: Report to the Medical Advisory Committee and quality committee
steps.description: The specialist summarizes the incident, findings and actions for the next Medical Advisory Committee meeting and adds it to the aggregated critical incident report the board quality committee receives at least twice a year.

control.basis: Public Hospitals Act, Regulation 965 (hospital management): disclosure of critical incidents to the patient, the medical advisory committee and the administrator

next.condition: medication or IV fluid critical incident

evidence.note: Aggregated critical incident data to the Quality Committee at least twice a year; disclosure to the MAC. Wait reflects monthly and quarterly committee calendars (author's estimate).

steps.name: Report the medication critical incident to NSIR
steps.description: The specialist enters the de-identified incident, harm level and contributing factors into CIHI's National System for Incident Reporting as the ministry directive requires for medication and IV fluid critical incidents, and answers any follow-up questions from ISMP Canada.

control.basis: Ontario Ministry of Health directive (October 2011) to report critical incidents involving medications and IV fluids to CIHI NSIR

evidence.note: Directive and NSIR reporting stated in both sources.

steps.name: Track completion of actions
steps.description: The specialist follows up each action owner until the change is in place (a new pump setting, a revised order set, a policy update), checks early evidence that it works and records completion in the incident file.

next.condition: a clinical system change is needed

evidence.note: Follow through and monitor effectiveness (CIAF). Durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Submit a system change request
steps.description: Where the fix needs a change to the hospital information system (an order set, an alert, a default dose), the specialist submits a change request to digital health with the incident reference and closes the incident file once it is accepted.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Close the incident file
steps.description: The specialist completes the closing fields in the incident system (final harm level, contributing factors, actions, disclosure dates) so the case counts in quarterly trend reports, and closes the file.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Critical incident with comprehensive review
exceptions.description: Death or serious harm not caused by the illness or a known risk: leaders are phoned at once, items secured, the patient told, a team review held under quality of care protection, and the case reported to the Medical Advisory Committee and the board quality committee.

exceptions.name: Medication critical incident reported to NSIR
exceptions.description: A medication or IV fluid critical incident is also entered in CIHI's national system under the 2011 ministry directive; Ontario hospitals together filed 17 such reports in 2015.

exceptions.name: Overdue manager follow-up
exceptions.description: The report sits in the manager's queue past the target and the quality specialist chases it, sometimes more than once.

exceptions.name: Serious event first rated as minor
exceptions.description: The screening specialist or the closing check finds harm or a pattern that the reporter or manager rated low and starts a preliminary review late.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from the incident to the report being closed
benchmarks.population: All incident reports at an Ontario community hospital, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: most reports wait one to three weeks for manager follow-up and a weekly closing check; serious incidents take one to three months, consistent with the CIAF's up-to-90-day comprehensive analysis. No published closure-time figure was found.
Stated in the source.

benchmarks.unit: share of reports that are serious events (harm)

evidence.note: 9,741 of 256,679 reports.

benchmarks.unit: reports to NSIR from all Ontario hospitals in 2015

evidence.note: Stated in the source.

pain_points.description: Reports wait in unit managers' queues for days or weeks because managers also run staffing, budgets and patient flow, so feedback to the reporter is slow.

evidence.note: Organisation file and author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Harm levels and incident types are misclassified at entry, so serious events can be missed until screening or closure.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Comprehensive reviews wait weeks for interviews and a meeting date that suits physicians, managers and staff, and committee reporting follows monthly and quarterly calendars.

evidence.note: CIAF allows up to 90 days for comprehensive analysis.

pain_points.description: Incident reports capture only part of the harm that occurs, and lessons are not shared between hospitals.

evidence.note: Auditor General found incident learning was not shared between hospitals; ISMP notes it cannot tell whether reported counts are complete.

sources.title: Acute-Care Hospital Patient Safety and Drug Administration (2019 Annual Report, Volume 1, Chapter 3, Section 3.01)
sources.publisher: Office of the Auditor General of Ontario
sources.supports: Ontario hospital patient safety governance: the CEO must establish a system for reviewing and disclosing critical incidents, implementing measures against recurrence and giving aggregated critical incident data to the board Quality Committee at least twice a year; a committee required by the Public Hospitals Act reviews critical incidents; optional Quality of Care Committee under QCIPA; staff are expected to report patient safety incidents; Accreditation Canada required practice on patient safety incident management; 154 medication critical incidents reported to NSIR from October 2011 to 2018; HIROC as insurer has access to incident cases.

sources.title: Ontario Hospital Critical Incidents Related to Medications or IV Fluids: Analysis Report, January to December 2015
sources.publisher: Institute for Safe Medication Practices Canada (for Health Quality Ontario)
sources.supports: October 2011 ministry directive that all critical incidents involving medications and IV fluids be reported to CIHI's National System for Incident Reporting; Regulation 965 definition of a critical incident; boards must ensure a system for analysing critical incidents and a plan to reduce recurrence; 17 such reports from all Ontario hospitals in 2015.

sources.title: Canadian Incident Analysis Framework
sources.publisher: Canadian Patient Safety Institute, ISMP Canada, Saskatchewan Health and Patients for Patient Safety Canada
sources.supports: Incident management stages: immediate response (care for patient, report, secure items, begin disclosure, reduce risk of recurrence), prepare for analysis (preliminary investigation, choose method, team, meetings, interviews), analysis, follow through, close the loop; concise analysis by one facilitator over hours to days for no or low harm; comprehensive analysis by an interdisciplinary team over up to 90 days; system versus accountability review triage.

sources.title: Policy B-301: Disclosing Adverse Events (revised January 2019)
sources.supports: Ontario community hospital practice: every adverse event documented in the chart and an incident report completed; significant harm reported to chief of staff, VP patient care and director of risk management, administrator on call after hours; disclosure in two stages (initial, then post-analysis) by the most responsible physician with a second person present; QCIPA limits what a quality of care review can disclose; facts of the disclosure recorded in the health record.

sources.title: 2022 Pennsylvania Patient Safety Reporting: Updated Rates for Acute Care Event Reports
sources.supports: Hospital event report rate of 27.9 reports per 1,000 patient days in 2022 in a mandatory statewide reporting system, the third annual decrease and 5.4% below 2021.

sources.title: Patient Safety Trends in 2022: An Analysis of 256,679 Serious Events and Incidents From the Nation's Largest Event Reporting Database
sources.publisher: Patient Safety (Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority), S. Kepner and R. Jones
sources.supports: Of 256,679 acute care reports in 2022, 96.2% were incidents (no harm) and 3.8% (9,741) serious events with harm; 489 (0.19%) were high harm.

sources.title: Safety Incident Management (harmonized policy)
sources.publisher: Huron Perth and Area Ontario Health Team
sources.supports: Ontario hospital policy: first priority is the immediate needs of the patient; all staff report incidents, hazards and near misses promptly, inform their supervisor and complete a report; incidents reviewed and tracked to identify trends; Public Hospitals Act definition of a critical incident.

assumptions: The reporting staff member is represented by the inpatient RN role (med_rn), and the managers of medicine, mental health, maternity, paediatrics and support units by med_manager; the most responsible physician is represented by the hospitalist role.
Immediate clinical care after the incident (s01) is counted here in short form; any treatment of injuries belongs to the clinical process.

About 3.5% of reports are phoned in as serious at once and a further 3% are upgraded at screening or closing, so about 6.5-7% get a preliminary review; about 0.6% of reports (roughly 40 a year) get a comprehensive review and about 0.6% (roughly 40 a year) are written up individually for the Medical Advisory Committee and quality committee; about one a year is a medication critical incident reported to NSIR, which is in line with harmful-event shares in a large mandatory system (3.8% harmful, 0.19% high harm).

Insurer notices, committee reports and disclosure letters are produced only on the serious-incident path (outcome closed_after_review); the quality_report to the quality improvement plan process is the aggregated trend data from every report.
Device-related incidents also go to biomedical engineering, which files Health Canada device reports in its own process; that handoff is not drawn here.

The simulated median cycle time is driven by the manager follow-up queue (mode five days, up to three weeks) and the weekly closing check; the 90th percentile includes chased reports and serious incidents that take one to three months.
Regulation 965 requirements are taken from the Auditor General and ISMP Canada descriptions; the provincial e-Laws page could not be opened, so no section numbers are cited.
